events.fact: The Battle of Gettysburg opened in Pennsylvania, where the Army of the Potomac under General George Meade met Robert E. Lee's invading army in the largest battle ever fought on American soil.
The Battle of San Juan Hill was fought in Cuba, where Colonel Theodore Roosevelt led his Rough Riders in the charge up Kettle Hill, the decisive land victory of the Spanish-American War.

block: On July 1, 1863, the Battle of Gettysburg opened in the Pennsylvania hills, where General George Meade's outnumbered men took the high ground and held it through three days that turned back Lee's invasion and saved the Union. On the same day in 1898, Colonel Theodore Roosevelt led his Rough Riders up San Juan Heights near Santiago, charging through withering fire to seize the ground and break Spanish resistance in Cuba. Both fields were won by men who would not flinch when the cost was steep, and a Steadfast citizen learns from them that the line is held not by the strong of body alone but by the steady of heart who trust God to sustain them in the hour of trial.

events.fact: Pickett's Charge, the climactic assault of the Battle of Gettysburg, was made and repulsed, marking the high-water mark of the Confederacy and the failure of Lee's invasion of the North.
President Benjamin Harrison signed the act admitting Idaho as the 43rd state of the Union.

block: On July 3, 1863, the third day at Gettysburg ended in Pickett's Charge, when fifteen thousand Confederate soldiers crossed nearly a mile of open ground into Union fire and were broken at the stone wall, the high-water mark of the rebellion and the turning of the war. On the same day in 1890, President Benjamin Harrison signed the act admitting Idaho as the forty-third state, drawing another commonwealth of the mountain frontier into the ordered Union. The one day saw a nation preserved by hard endurance and the other a nation enlarged in peace, and a Steadfast citizen presses on through both the costly fight and the patient labor, knowing the Lord establishes the work of faithful hands.

events.fact: The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence in Philadelphia, formally proclaiming the thirteen colonies free and independent states.
Former presidents John Adams and Thomas Jefferson both died on the fiftieth anniversary of the Declaration, Jefferson at Monticello and Adams at Quincy hours later.

block: On July 4, 1776, the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence at Philadelphia, pledging lives, fortunes, and sacred honor upon the truth that men are endowed by their Creator with unalienable rights. By the remarkable providence of God, on the same day fifty years later in 1826, John Adams and Thomas Jefferson, the document's great advocate and its author, both passed from this life within hours of each other, Jefferson at Monticello and Adams at Quincy, his last thoughts upon his old friend. That two founders should be summoned home on the jubilee of their labor reminds a Steadfast citizen that a man finishes his course and lays it down, but the cause he serves in faith endures long after him under the hand of the God who raised it up.

events.fact: The United States Secret Service was organized as a division of the Treasury Department, founded under Chief William P. Wood to suppress the rampant counterfeiting that threatened the postwar economy.
David Glasgow Farragut, who would become the U.S. Navy's first admiral and the hero of Mobile Bay, was born near Knoxville, Tennessee.

block: On July 5, 1865, the United States Secret Service was established under the Treasury to hunt down the counterfeiters whose false money had corrupted nearly a third of the nation's currency, a quiet labor to guard the people's honest trust. On the same day in 1801, David Glasgow Farragut was born in Tennessee, the sailor who at Mobile Bay would lash himself to the rigging and cry, 'Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead,' driving his fleet through the mines to victory. The one defends the integrity of a coin and the other the safety of a fleet, and a Steadfast citizen holds his post with the same resolve, guarding what is true and pressing forward where lesser men would turn back.

events.fact: John Paul Jones, the Revolutionary naval commander remembered as a father of the United States Navy, was born in Kirkbean, Scotland.
The Continental Congress established the dollar as the official monetary unit of the United States, adopting a decimal system based on the Spanish silver dollar.

block: On July 6, 1747, John Paul Jones was born in Scotland, the captain who, his ship shot through and sinking beneath him, answered the demand to surrender with the immortal words, 'I have not yet begun to fight,' and went on to take the Serapis. On the same day in 1785, the Continental Congress fixed the dollar as the coin of the young Republic, laying an honest and orderly foundation for the commerce of a free people. The one secured the nation's honor at sea and the other its honest dealing at home, and a Steadfast citizen marries the two, refusing to quit the fight and refusing to corrupt the trust, faithful in great things and small before the Lord.

events.fact: Commodore John D. Sloat raised the American flag over the Custom House at Monterey, taking formal possession of California for the United States during the Mexican-American War.
The conspirators convicted in the assassination of President Abraham Lincoln were hanged at the Washington Arsenal after trial by military commission.

block: On July 7, 1846, Commodore John D. Sloat sailed into Monterey and raised the Stars and Stripes over the Custom House, claiming California for the United States without the firing of a shot. On the same day in 1865, the conspirators in the murder of President Lincoln met justice on the gallows at the Washington Arsenal, the lawful end of the men who had struck down the Republic's leader in the hour of victory. The one extended a free nation to the Pacific shore and the other answered bloodshed with the measured judgment of law, and a Steadfast citizen holds the line on both, advancing what is good and standing firm that wrong shall not go unanswered, as the God of justice requires.

events.fact: The Declaration of Independence received its first public reading in the State House yard at Philadelphia by Colonel John Nixon, as the bells of the city, including the State House bell, rang out.
The first issue of The Wall Street Journal was published by Charles Dow and Edward Jones in New York City.

block: On July 8, 1776, Colonel John Nixon stood in the State House yard at Philadelphia and read the Declaration of Independence aloud for the first time to a gathered crowd, while the bells of the city pealed and the people answered with loud huzzas. On the same day in 1889, Charles Dow and Edward Jones printed the first four-page issue of The Wall Street Journal, beginning a faithful chronicle of the nation's honest commerce and industry. The one proclaimed a people's liberty and the other served the daily labor of free men, and a Steadfast citizen values both the ringing word that founds a nation and the patient work that sustains it, holding fast to the God-given liberty his fathers won.

events.fact: General George Washington ordered the Declaration of Independence read aloud to the assembled Continental Army in New York to steel his soldiers for the coming struggle.
President Zachary Taylor, hero of the Mexican-American War, died in office in Washington after a brief illness, and Vice President Millard Fillmore succeeded him.

block: On July 9, 1776, General George Washington had the newly arrived Declaration of Independence read to his Continental Army on the parade grounds of Lower Manhattan, that the men facing a mighty enemy might know the great cause for which they would fight and perhaps die. On the same day in 1850, President Zachary Taylor, the old soldier whom the nation had lately raised to its highest office, was taken by sudden illness, and the Republic submitted to the loss as Millard Fillmore quietly took up the office. The one steeled men for a long fight and the other bowed before the providence that numbers a man's days, and a Steadfast citizen learns to stand firm in the cause and to trust the God who holds both the soldier's courage and the leader's appointed end.

events.fact: President Benjamin Harrison signed the act admitting Wyoming as the 44th state of the Union.
President Andrew Jackson vetoed the bill to recharter the Second Bank of the United States, issuing a message defending the equal rights of the common citizen against concentrated privilege.

block: On July 10, 1890, President Benjamin Harrison signed the act that admitted Wyoming as the forty-fourth state, bringing the high plains of the West under the ordered government of the Union. On the same day in 1832, President Andrew Jackson vetoed the recharter of the Second Bank, declaring that government must dispense its favors with an even hand and not bend the law to the benefit of the powerful few. The one brought a frontier people lawfully into the nation's house and the other defended the plain rule of equal justice, and an Obedient citizen submits gladly to lawful order while insisting, under God, that the law bind every man alike.

events.fact: John Quincy Adams, sixth president of the United States and a lifelong diplomat and statesman, was born in Braintree (now Quincy), Massachusetts.
Vice President Aaron Burr mortally wounded former Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton in their duel at Weehawken, New Jersey; Hamilton died the following day.

block: On July 11, 1767, John Quincy Adams was born at Braintree in Massachusetts, son of a president and a tireless servant of his country who, long after the White House, would die at his post in the House of Representatives defending the right. On the same day in 1804, Vice President Aaron Burr met Alexander Hamilton with pistols at Weehawken and shot the great architect of the nation's finances, who died the next day, a needless loss born of wounded pride. The one shows a life poured out in steady duty and the other a brilliant man undone in a single rash hour, and a Steadfast citizen marks the difference, choosing the long faithful course over the passion of the moment, for the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.

events.fact: President Abraham Lincoln signed the resolution of Congress creating the U.S. Army Medal of Honor, the nation's highest award for valor in combat.
George Eastman, the inventor and industrialist whose roll film and Kodak camera brought photography to ordinary Americans, was born in Waterville, New York.

block: On July 12, 1862, President Abraham Lincoln signed into law the resolution establishing the Army Medal of Honor, that the Republic might forever set apart and remember the men who distinguish themselves by gallantry above and beyond the call of duty. On the same day in 1854, George Eastman was born in New York, the inventor whose roll film and simple camera would place the gift of capturing a moment into the hands of every common man. The one honors the soldier who answers a high responsibility with his very life and the other an honest craftsman who labored to serve his neighbor, and a Responsible citizen embraces both burdens, the duty entrusted to him and the work set before him, as unto the Lord who gives every man his charge.

events.fact: The Confederation Congress enacted the Northwest Ordinance, chartering government for the territory north of the Ohio River, providing a path to statehood, guaranteeing civil liberties, and dedicating land to public schools.
The American explorer Henry Rowe Schoolcraft reached the true source of the Mississippi River at Lake Itasca in present-day Minnesota.

block: On July 13, 1787, the Confederation Congress passed the Northwest Ordinance, the great charter of the frontier that opened an orderly road to statehood, secured the liberties of settlers, forbade slavery in the territory, and set aside land for schools because, as it declared, religion, morality, and knowledge are necessary to good government. On the same day in 1832, the explorer Henry Schoolcraft pressed through lakes and portages to stand at last at Lake Itasca, the true headwaters of the Mississippi he had long sought. The one laid a wise foundation for new commonwealths and the other reached the end of a long search, and a Steadfast citizen labors in the same spirit, building for generations he will not see and pressing on until the appointed work is finished, trusting the God who blesses faithful perseverance.

events.fact: Gerald R. Ford, the 38th president of the United States, was born in Omaha, Nebraska.
Congress passed the Sedition Act, part of the Alien and Sedition Acts, whose overreach against free speech provoked a constitutional reckoning that strengthened the people's liberties.

block: On July 14, 1913, Gerald R. Ford was born in Omaha, the steady and unassuming man who would be called to the presidency in a season of national crisis and labored to bind up the country's wounds with plain honesty. On the same day in 1798, a fearful Congress passed the Sedition Act, reaching too far against the freedom of speech, an overreach the people answered until the right of free expression stood the stronger for the contest. The one shows a leader's quiet integrity and the other a republic correcting its own excess, and a Steadfast citizen stands firm for liberty in both, knowing that the truth endures and that the God who governs the nations upholds the cause of the just.

events.fact: Lieutenant Zebulon Pike set out from near St. Louis on his expedition to explore the southwestern reaches of the Louisiana Purchase, in the course of which he sighted the peak that bears his name.
William E. Boeing founded the Pacific Aero Products Company in Seattle, the aircraft enterprise that would become the Boeing Company.

block: On July 15, 1806, Lieutenant Zebulon Pike set out from the Missouri country to chart the far southwestern reaches of the new Louisiana Purchase, an arduous journey through unknown mountains in which he marked the towering summit men still call Pikes Peak. On the same day in 1916, William Boeing founded his small aircraft company in Seattle, a venture begun in a wooden boathouse that would one day carry the nation aloft. The one ventured into the wilderness and the other into the untried sky, and an Enduring citizen presses forward as they did, undaunted by the long road or the heavy odds, trusting the God who goes before His people into every frontier.

events.fact: The first atomic bomb was detonated in the Trinity test at the Jornada del Muerto desert in New Mexico, opening the nuclear age.
Apollo 11 launched from Kennedy Space Center in Florida atop a Saturn V rocket, carrying Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins toward the first manned landing on the Moon.

block: On July 16, 1945, the first atomic device was detonated before dawn in the New Mexico desert at the Trinity site, a fearsome unleashing of nature's hidden power that sobered even the men who made it. On the same day in 1969, Apollo 11 rose from Cape Kennedy on a pillar of fire, bearing Armstrong, Aldrin, and Collins on the long voyage to the Moon. The one revealed the terrible reach of man's knowledge and the other its noblest ambition, and a Steadfast citizen presses on in his own calling with sober reverence, remembering that every power and every height belongs first to the God who set the heavens in their order.

events.fact: Spain formally transferred Florida to the United States at Pensacola under the Adams-Onis Treaty, and Andrew Jackson took possession as the first territorial governor.
Walt Disney opened Disneyland in Anaheim, California, the first theme park built under his direct supervision.

block: On July 17, 1821, Spain handed Florida to the United States in a solemn ceremony at Pensacola, completing by treaty and law the orderly addition of the peninsula to the Republic, with Andrew Jackson sworn as its first governor. On the same day in 1955, Walt Disney opened the gates of Disneyland in California, the fruit of a craftsman's long labor and bold imagination. The one shows a nation enlarged by lawful covenant and the other a man's honest enterprise rewarded, and an Obedient citizen honors both the rule of law that orders a people and the diligent work done well, submitting his own labors to the God who blesses what is built in good faith.

events.fact: John Paul Jones, the Revolutionary naval hero and father of the United States Navy, died in Paris at the age of forty-five; his remains were later returned to rest at the Naval Academy at Annapolis.
President Harry Truman signed the Presidential Succession Act, fixing the orderly line of succession to the presidency through the Speaker of the House and the president pro tempore of the Senate.

block: On July 18, 1792, John Paul Jones died in a Paris apartment, far from the nation he had served, the indomitable captain whose victories at sea had given the young Republic its first naval glory; a century later American warships bore him home to honored rest at Annapolis. On the same day in 1947, President Harry Truman signed the Presidential Succession Act, establishing through elected officers the lawful and orderly passing of the highest office should it fall vacant. The one gave his strength to defend the nation and the other secured the peaceful continuance of its government, and an Obedient citizen reveres both the warrior's faithful service and the settled rule of law, taking his own ordered place under the authority God has appointed.

events.fact: On the Lewis and Clark expedition, Captain Meriwether Lewis led the party through the dramatic limestone canyon of the Missouri River he named the Gates of the Mountains in present-day Montana.
Apollo 11 fired its engine and entered orbit around the Moon, the crew passing over the Sea of Tranquility where they would land the following day.

block: On July 19, 1805, Captain Meriwether Lewis guided his expedition's canoes through a towering rock gorge of the Missouri River, naming it the Gates of the Mountains, pressing ever westward through an unmapped continent toward the Pacific. On the same day in 1969, Apollo 11 slipped behind the Moon and fired its engine to enter lunar orbit, circling the gray plains where Armstrong and Aldrin would soon descend. The one was a stubborn overland journey of years and the other a voyage across the void of space, yet both were the triumph of men who would not turn back, and a Steadfast citizen presses on through his own long road, trusting the God who upholds those who endure to the end.

events.fact: The Apollo 11 lunar module Eagle landed in the Sea of Tranquility, and Neil Armstrong became the first man to set foot on the Moon, declaring it one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.
The Viking 1 lander touched down on Mars, the first American spacecraft to land successfully on the surface of another planet and return data.

block: On July 20, 1969, the lunar module Eagle settled onto the Sea of Tranquility, and Neil Armstrong stepped down onto the Moon with the words, 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind,' as half a billion souls watched below. On the same day in 1976, the Viking 1 lander came to rest on the red plains of Mars, the first American craft to touch another planet and send back its findings. Both were the crown of countless men's patient toil over many years, and a Steadfast citizen labors with the same long endurance in his own appointed work, lifting his eyes in wonder to the God whose heavens declare His glory.

events.fact: The First Battle of Bull Run (First Manassas) was fought in Virginia, the first major land battle of the Civil War, shattering Northern hopes of a quick and easy victory.
The NS Savannah, the first nuclear-powered merchant ship, was christened and launched as part of President Eisenhower's Atoms for Peace program.

block: On July 21, 1861, the armies clashed along Bull Run near Manassas in Virginia, the first great battle of the Civil War, where raw and untried men learned in blood that the struggle would be long and the cost beyond all reckoning. On the same day in 1959, the NS Savannah, the first nuclear merchant ship, slid into the water, a peaceful turning of the atom's power toward honest trade. The one taught a people to gird themselves for hard endurance and the other showed industry bending great power to the good of men, and a Steadfast citizen settles in for the long labor before him, neither dismayed by the cost nor idle in the calling God has given.

events.fact: The Battle of Atlanta was fought in Georgia, where Union forces under William T. Sherman repulsed John Bell Hood's army; Major General James B. McPherson was killed leading from the front.
The aviator Wiley Post completed the first solo flight around the world, returning to New York after circling the globe in under eight days.

block: On July 22, 1864, the Battle of Atlanta raged southeast of the city, where Sherman's men threw back Hood's desperate assault, though at the cost of the gallant General James McPherson, who fell as he rode forward to his lines. On the same day in 1933, Wiley Post brought his weary plane down at New York, having flown alone around the entire world in less than eight days, a feat of grit no man had achieved by himself before. The one shows a soldier spending his life in the front rank and the other a flyer enduring exhaustion and danger to finish a near-impossible course, and a Steadfast citizen holds fast in his own trial, pressing on to the last mile in the strength the Lord supplies.

events.fact: William Austin Burt of Michigan received the U.S. patent for his typographer, the forerunner of the typewriter, the document signed by President Andrew Jackson.
Ulysses S. Grant, victorious Union general and eighteenth president, died of throat cancer at Mount McGregor, New York, days after completing the memoirs he wrote to provide for his family.

block: On July 23, 1829, William Burt of the Michigan frontier received the first American patent for a writing machine, his typographer, the seed of the typewriter that would one day transform every office in the land. On the same day in 1885, Ulysses S. Grant died of his long and painful illness at Mount McGregor, having driven himself in his final weeks to finish his memoirs and so leave his family secure, completing the manuscript only days before the end. The one labored to invent and the other labored to the very edge of the grave to fulfill his duty, and a Steadfast citizen honors both, working with diligent hands and finishing the task set before him no matter the cost, faithful to the God who measures every man's labor.

events.fact: Brigham Young led the first company of Mormon pioneers into the Salt Lake Valley after a journey of more than a thousand miles, declaring it the place to settle.
The Apollo 11 crew splashed down safely in the Pacific Ocean, completing the first manned voyage to the Moon and returning home.

block: On July 24, 1847, after seventeen months and more than a thousand miles of hardship across the plains and mountains, Brigham Young looked out over the desolate Salt Lake Valley and judged it the place where his weary people would at last settle and build. On the same day in 1969, the astronauts of Apollo 11 dropped from the sky into the Pacific, their voyage to the Moon complete and their long journey safely ended. The one was an exhausting trek to a promised refuge and the other a return home across a quarter million miles, and an Enduring citizen takes heart from both, bearing the long road with patience and arriving at last by the mercy of the God who brings His travelers safely to their rest.

events.fact: Congress promoted Ulysses S. Grant to the newly created rank of General of the Army, making him the first American to hold a four-star general's commission.
President Andrew Johnson signed the Wyoming Organic Act, creating the Wyoming Territory and establishing lawful government over its frontier lands.

block: On July 25, 1866, a grateful Congress raised Ulysses S. Grant to the new rank of General of the Army, the first four-star general in the nation's history, entrusting the whole weight of its arms to the man who had carried it to victory. On the same day in 1868, President Andrew Johnson signed the act creating the Wyoming Territory, laying ordered government over a vast and unsettled frontier. The one placed a great responsibility upon a proven man and the other established the careful stewardship of new lands, and a Responsible citizen bears his own charge in the same spirit, accepting the duty laid upon him and tending faithfully what God has put into his keeping.

events.fact: New York ratified the United States Constitution by a narrow vote at Poughkeepsie, becoming the eleventh state and securing the new federal government.
The Second Continental Congress established the American postal system and appointed Benjamin Franklin the first Postmaster General.

block: On July 26, 1788, after fierce debate, New York ratified the Constitution by the slim margin of thirty votes to twenty-seven, becoming the eleventh state and giving the new union the assent it sorely needed to stand. On the same day in 1775, the Continental Congress founded the American post and named Benjamin Franklin the first Postmaster General, binding the scattered colonies together with reliable communication in the cause of liberty. The one shows free men submitting themselves to a common frame of government and the other a faithful servant ordering the bonds that held a people together, and an Obedient citizen honors both, taking his place under lawful authority and serving the common good as unto the God who ordains good order.

events.fact: The Korean War Armistice was signed at Panmunjom, ending three years of fighting and establishing the demilitarized zone between North and South Korea.
President George Washington signed the act establishing the Department of Foreign Affairs, soon renamed the Department of State, the first federal agency created under the new Constitution.

block: On July 27, 1953, after the longest armistice talks in history, the guns at last fell silent in Korea as the truce was signed at Panmunjom, the hard-won fruit of soldiers who had held the line through three brutal years of war. On the same day in 1789, President George Washington signed into being the Department of State, the first agency of the new federal government, the steady beginning of the institutions that would carry the Republic forward. The one shows endurance through a long and costly conflict and the other the patient founding of a lasting government, and a Steadfast citizen perseveres in both the fight and the building, trusting the God who establishes the work of those who do not grow weary in well-doing.

events.fact: President Dwight Eisenhower signed the National Aeronautics and Space Act, establishing NASA to lead the nation's peaceful exploration of space.
The first transcontinental telephone line was completed and tested, joining New York to San Francisco by voice across the breadth of the continent.

block: On July 29, 1958, President Eisenhower signed the act that created NASA, setting the United States upon the great peaceful endeavor to explore the heavens and reach the Moon. On the same day in 1914, the first transcontinental telephone line was completed, and a voice spoke clear across the whole continent from New York to San Francisco, the crowning achievement of years of dogged labor stringing wire over mountain and desert. The one launched a nation toward the stars and the other knit it together coast to coast, and a Steadfast citizen presses on in his own work with the same patient resolve, laboring step by step toward ends worthy of the God who gives men the wit and will to build.

events.fact: The first representative legislative assembly in English America, the House of Burgesses, convened in the church at Jamestown, Virginia.
President Dwight Eisenhower signed the law making 'In God We Trust' the official national motto of the United States.

block: On July 30, 1619, the House of Burgesses gathered in the little church at Jamestown, the first representative assembly in English America, and among its earliest acts it enjoined honest dealing and the keeping of the Sabbath, planting the seed of ordered self-government on this continent. On the same day in 1956, President Eisenhower signed the law that made 'In God We Trust' the official motto of the United States, declaring before the world the nation's confidence in its Maker. The one founded a people's rule under law and the other confessed the higher Lord above all law, and an Obedient citizen submits to both, governing himself uprightly while trusting wholly in the God whose name the nation has placed upon its very coin.

events.fact: The first United States patent was issued to Samuel Hopkins for an improved process of making potash, signed by President George Washington.
The Continental Congress commissioned the young Marquis de Lafayette a major general in the Continental Army, a rank he accepted to serve without pay.

block: On July 31, 1790, the United States issued its very first patent, granted to Samuel Hopkins of Philadelphia for a better method of making potash and signed by President Washington himself, rewarding honest ingenuity in the new Republic. On the same day in 1777, Congress commissioned the nineteen-year-old Marquis de Lafayette a major general, a rank the young Frenchman took up freely and without pay for love of the American cause. The one honors the inventor who labors to better his trade and the other the volunteer who gives himself wholly to a cause not his own, and a Steadfast citizen joins them in faithful perseverance, working and serving without thought of ease, as unto the God who rewards every diligent hand.
